question.text:
2 ′′
How many twice continuously differentiable functions on (−1, 1) satisfy x y − 2y = 0 at every
′
point and y(0) = y (0) = 0?
(A) None. (B) Exactly one. (C) Exactly two. (D) Exactly three. (E) Infinitely many.

solution.text:
2
The indicial equation is m(m − 1) − 2 = (m − 2)(m + 1) = 0. In particular, y = Cx is a
twice continuously differentiable solution on the whole interval for every real C, and each
2
satisfies the two initial conditions. Thus there are infinitely many. Dividing by x produces
a coefficient singular at the initial point, so the ordinary uniqueness theorem cannot be
applied there.
